newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary outlines plans to boost small/medium firms.
newsitem.headline: Hungary outlines plans to boost small/medium firms.

text.p: Hungary outlined on Friday a government programme to invest in the country's small and medium sized businesses, particularly as suppliers to foreign companies operating in the country.

Finance Minister Peter Megyessy said the four-tier policy covered state investment in private firms, pushing Hungarian investment abroad, boosting supply contracts with foreign manufacturers and giving priority to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in public procurement contracts.

"To promote venture capital, the government should take stakes in SMEs of up to 30 percent," Medgyessy told a conference on small and medium enterprises in Budapest on Friday. "These will be defined in the 1998 budget."

As a means of encouraging Hungarian investment abroad the state-owned Hungarian Development Bank and Eximbank will put up one billion forints as start-up equity in a fund which will supplement Hungarian capital used outside the country, Medgyessy said.
He also said the government and foreign companies both recognised the need for SMEs to become subcontractors to large foreign firms.
"We are already in negotations with a number of significant foreign companies to launch a local supplier programme," he said.

Industry Minister Szabolcs Fazakas told the conference that most new foreign investors were now establishing greenfield ventures to manufacture and export from Hungary and cited Sony and General Motors, which produces Opel Astras in Hungary, as looking to expand their Hungarian suppliers.
"General Motors has indicated its plans for a future spare parts progroamme while Sony would like to set up a regional distribution centre in Hungary with 200 interested suppliers," he said.
A total of 350 Hungarian companies currently supply parts for car manufacturing while 200 Hungarian companies supply the electronics production sector.
Szabolcs also announced an expanding programme of loan interest subsidies for small firms, who face crippling domestic interest rates of up to 40 percent.
"The subsidies will reduce rates from 40 percent to 20 percent in five percent steps while poorer regions and depressed industries will get an even higher subsidy," he said.
He added that the government had reached agreement with 27 Hungarian and foreign banks on interest subsidy schemes

While SMEs -- defined as businesses employing 11 to 50 employees -- current total around 18,000, Hungarian trade ministry figures put the number of micro-businesses of one to 10 employees at over one million.
Most of these are economically inactive and were founded in the early 1990s to benefit from VAT tax exemptions.

"In order for more of these companies to become active we need to develop an enterpise culture through information on how to get started and where to get investment," he said, adding that the government's Regional Development Agency had drawn up a "credit map" guiding SMEs towards over 80 sources of credit.
Medgyessy also pledged to reduce current rates of company tax in next year's budget.
